title: Lesson 3: Advanced Hermes Configuration: Model Routing, Evals, and Guardrails in Production
description: When the agent leaves the sandbox and runs at real volume in front of a client, three decisions decide whether it holds up: which model runs which task, how you prove the output is still correct, and how you keep the guardrails you documented actually enforced. This lesson teaches all three.

questions.question: What is the main problem with running every task on one model?
options: It makes the provider and env configuration harder to manage
It overpays easy work and underperforms hard work
It caps the number of scheduled jobs the agent can run
It forces every task onto the cheapest available model
questions.explanation: A single default treats trivial and demanding work as equal, so the easy task overpays and the hard task runs on a model too weak for it.

questions.question: What is the purpose of an eval suite built from known-good cases?
options: To make every scheduled run finish more quickly
To remove the need for a human to review output
To catch silent regressions when inputs change
To record every command the agent issues in a log
questions.explanation: A fixed set of known-good cases with expected outputs catches the quiet degradation that a rule, data, or model change can introduce.

questions.question: When an unattended run meets a dangerous command and no one is present to approve it, what is the safe default?
options: Approve it automatically so the run completes
Skip the check and log a warning instead
Retry the command on a stronger model
Deny it so the run stops or diverts
questions.explanation: A headless run should fail closed: blocking the command is the safe default, while auto-approval is reserved for a fully trusted, isolated environment.
